user_input: Can you prove de Morgan's law using Gentzen inference rules for intuitionistic logic?
model_output:
De Morgan's law is a mathematical principle that states that the negation of a disjunction is equivalent to the conjunction of the negations of the disjuncts, and the negation of a conjunction is equivalent to the disjunction of the negations of the conjuncts. In other words, it can be expressed as:
(A ∨ B) → (¬A ∧ ¬B)
(A ∧ B) → (¬A ∨ ¬B)
Here is a proof of De Morgan's law using Gentzen inference rules for intuitionistic logic:
1. A → (B ∨ C)
2. ¬A → ¬(B ∨ C) [by contraposition]
3. ¬(B ∨ C) → ¬B ∧ ¬C [by Gentzen rule]
4. ¬B ∧ ¬C → ¬(B ∧ C) [by substitution]
5. ¬(B ∧ C) → (¬B ∨ ¬C) [by Gentzen rule]
6. (¬B ∨ ¬C) → ¬B ∧ ¬C [by substitution]
7. ¬B ∧ ¬C → ¬A [by Gentzen rule]
8. ¬A → (B ∨ C) [by substitution]
9. (B ∨ C) → (¬A ∧ ¬B) [by De Morgan's law]
10. (B ∨ C) → (¬A ∨ ¬B) [by De Morgan's law]
11. ¬A ∧ ¬B → (B ∨ C) [by Gentzen rule]
12. ¬A ∧ ¬B → ¬(B ∧ C) [by Gentzen rule]
13. ¬(B ∧ C) → ¬B ∧ ¬C [by Gentzen rule]
14. ¬B ∧ ¬C → ¬(B ∧ C) [by substitution]
15. ¬(B ∧ C) → (¬B ∨ ¬C) [by Gentzen rule]
16. (¬B ∨ ¬C) → ¬(B ∧ C) [by substitution]
